title: Given an array where each element is the maximum jump length from that position, determine whether you can reach the last index starting from the first.
shortTitle: Jump Game — can you reach the last index (greedy reachability)

s1_definition.profdef: Greedy reachability: track the farthest index reachable so far. Iterate left to right; if the current index exceeds the farthest reach, return false; otherwise extend reach to max(reach, i + nums[i]). Reachable if reach eventually covers the last index. Time O(n), space O(1).
s1_definition.analogy: A settlement pipeline at National Bank of India has stages, and each stage lists how many stages ahead it can skip to. An operator walks forward tracking the farthest stage currently reachable; if he ever stands beyond that frontier he is stuck, otherwise he can finish.
s1_definition.oneliner: Track farthest reach; if i > reach you are stuck; else extend reach.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Greedy reachability: track the farthest index reachable so far. Iterate left to right; if the current index exceeds the farthest reach, return false; otherwise extend reach to max(reach, i + nums[i]). Reachable if reach eventually covers the last index. Time O(n), space O(1).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A settlement pipeline at National Bank of India has stages, and each stage lists how many stages ahead it can skip to. An operator walks forward tracking the farthest stage currently reachable; if he ever stands beyond that frontier he is stuck, otherwise he can finish.

**One line to remember:** Track farthest reach; if i > reach you are stuck; else extend reach.

sections.s2_technical:
Keep a single variable reach starting at zero, the farthest index you can get to. Walk i from zero to the last index. At each step, if i is greater than reach you can never have arrived here, so return false. Otherwise update reach to the maximum of its current value and i plus nums[i]. For example: `if (i > reach) return false; reach = Math.max(reach, i + nums[i]);`.

The greedy works because reachability is monotone: if you can reach index i you can reach any index up to reach, so you only ever need the single farthest frontier, not which exact path got there. If the loop finishes without getting stuck, the last index is reachable.

The time is O(n) and space is O(1). A senior nuance is that this is far cheaper than the equivalent O(n²) DP where dp[i] marks reachability from each prior jumpable index; the greedy frontier collapses that whole table into one number.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a settlement pipeline has stages where each stage declares how many stages ahead it can skip, and operations must know if the final stage is reachable from the start. This is exactly how Jump Game works.

Problem 2 — Trying every jump combination is exponential and needless. This is exactly why a single greedy reachability frontier is enough.

The mini-project builds a `PipelineReachability`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input jumps are two, three, one, one, four.

Step 1: Reach starts at zero at index zero, then extends to two because index zero plus two is two.

Step 2: At index one, since one is within reach, reach extends to four because one plus three is four.

Step 3: Indices two and three are within reach and do not extend the frontier beyond four.

Step 4: At index four the reach already covers the last index, so the walk finishes successfully.

Step 5: For three, two, one, zero, four the frontier stalls at three and index four lies beyond it, so it returns false.

```text
2026-10-27T03:00:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Pipeline Reachability (Jump Game)
2026-10-27T03:00:00Z [INFO] Last stage reachable
2026-10-27T03:00:00Z [INFO] {2,3,1,1,4} → true
2026-10-27T03:00:00Z [WARNING] Stuck: cannot pass index 3
2026-10-27T03:00:00Z [INFO] {3,2,1,0,4} → false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  jumps = 2 3 1 1 4
  i=0 reach=max(0,0+2)=2
  i=1 reach=max(2,1+3)=4
  i=2 reach=max(4,2+1)=4
  i=3 reach=max(4,3+1)=4  (covers last index 4) → true
  stuck case: reach frozen at 3, i=4 > 3 → false
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Jump Game is a greedy reachability problem. I keep a single variable for the farthest index I can reach so far and walk the array left to right. At each index, if the index is already beyond my farthest reach then I could never have arrived there and I return false; otherwise I extend the reach to the maximum of its current value and the index plus the jump available there.

The greedy is correct because reachability is monotone: if I can reach some index I can reach everything up to my current frontier, so I never need to know which exact path got me there, only the single farthest point. If the walk completes without getting stranded, the last index is reachable.

In my project at National Bank of India, a settlement pipeline had stages where each stage declared how many stages ahead it could skip, and operations needed to know if the final stage was reachable from the start. Rather than trying every jump combination, which is exponential, I used this constant-space greedy frontier, and I point out in interviews that it collapses the equivalent quadratic reachability DP into one number.
